Classifying vegetation surveys with RESY

Florian Jansen, Markus Bauer, Mariasole Calbi & Gilles Colling

RESY.Rmd

Introduction

RESY implements the Expert System (ESy) framework for vegetation classification (Bruelheide 1997; Chytrý et al. 2020). An ESy file encodes three sections:

  1. Taxonomy – species aggregations and synonyms
  2. Taxon groups – species assemblages referenced in classification conditions
  3. Vegetation types – logical formulas that combine group thresholds into named habitat types

The package can work with any ESy-compliant classification. This vignette uses two bundled systems:

  • EUNIS (European Nature Information System habitat types; FloraVeg.EU)
  • Apennine-test (a simplified test system for the Italian Apennines)

Many EUNIS rules also use site data from the header table (Ecoreg, Country, Coast_EEA, Dunes_Bohn). vignette("EUNIS") shows how to add these columns.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(RESY)

1. Load and prepare species data

resy_classify() expects the observation table to have one row per species in each plot, with three columns. Each column can also have its Darwin Core name, the standard set of field names for biodiversity data:

Column Darwin Core name Description
PlotObservationID eventID Plot identifier
TaxonName scientificName Species name
Cover_Perc organismQuantity, with organismQuantityType "% cover" Cover of the species in percent

For a species column with any other name, set species_col. The example data uses scientificName.

data_species <- read_csv(
  system.file("extdata", "data_example_species.csv", package = "RESY"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

glimpse(data_species)
#> Rows: 3,580
#> Columns: 3
#> $ PlotObservationID <chr> "HU32", "HU32", "HU32", "HU32", "HU32", "HU32", "HU3…
#> $ Cover_Perc        <dbl> 0.1, 0.1, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 87.5, 3.0, 3.0, 3.0, 0…
#> $ scientificName    <chr> "Dryopteris filix-mas (L.) Schott", "Cephalanthera l…

The header table has one row per plot, with the plot ID and the site data the rules use, such as the country or the altitude. Apennine-test uses no site data, so here the header table contains only the plot IDs, but resy_classify() still requires it. It must contain the same plot ID column as the observation table.

header <- data_species |>
  distinct(PlotObservationID) |>
  as.data.frame()

2. Load expert systems

resy_available_classifications() lists the schemes and versions bundled with the package.

resy_available_classifications() |> select(scheme, version)
#>          scheme    version
#> 1 Apennine-test 2026-06-27
#> 2         EUNIS 2025-10-03

To add your own expert system, use resy_add_classification().

resy_load_expert() reads a bundled expert system into a resy_parsed_expert object, which the taxonomy check below uses. resy_classify() does not need this object: it loads the expert system itself from scheme and version.

parsed_apennine <- resy_load_expert(scheme = "Apennine-test")

The types of an expert system form a hierarchy. resy_expert_tree() prints it; fill = TRUE adds the group levels that the type codes imply but the expert system does not list:

tree_filled <- resy_expert_tree(parsed_apennine, fill = TRUE)
print(tree_filled)
#> <resy_expert_tree> 5 node(s), 2 top-level
#> F Forest
#>   FB Beech-fir montane forest
#> N Non-forest
#>   NG Nardus acidic grassland
#>   NS Sub-Mediterranean scrub and woodland

Apennine-test has two top-level types, forest (F) and non-forest (N), each with lower-level types. To browse the hierarchy in the browser, use resy_view_expert().

3. Check taxonomy

resy_check_taxonomy() checks the species names of the observation table against the species list of the expert system, including its synonyms. Each expert system has its own list, so a name can match in one system and not in another. The result has one row per distinct name: scientificName is the name as submitted, TaxonName the canonical name the classifier uses (NA when unmatched), and matched whether it was found. Printing it lists what each column holds and how many names matched.

tax_apennine <- resy_check_taxonomy(obs = data_species, parsed = parsed_apennine)
tax_apennine
#> <resy_taxa> 1009 name(s) from column `scientificName` checked against 950 Section 1 species
#>   scientificName  Name as submitted
#>   TaxonName       Canonical name used by resy_classify(); NA when unmatched
#>   matched         TRUE if found as a canonical name or Section 1 synonym
#> 1009 matched (100.0%), 0 unmatched
#> 
#>                                          scientificName
#> 1                      Dryopteris filix-mas (L.) Schott
#> 2                 Cephalanthera longifolia (L.) Fritsch
#> 3                                Prenanthes purpurea L.
#> 4                                   Anemone nemorosa L.
#> 5  Epipactis helleborine (L.) Crantz subsp. helleborine
#> 6                  Sorbus aucuparia L. subsp. aucuparia
#> 7                                    Fagus sylvatica L.
#> 8                           Rubus hirtus Waldst. & Kit.
#> 9                                      Abies alba Mill.
#> 10                                 Oxalis acetosella L.
#>                   TaxonName matched
#> 1      Dryopteris filix-mas    TRUE
#> 2  Cephalanthera longifolia    TRUE
#> 3       Prenanthes purpurea    TRUE
#> 4          Anemone nemorosa    TRUE
#> 5     Epipactis helleborine    TRUE
#> 6          Sorbus aucuparia    TRUE
#> 7           Fagus sylvatica    TRUE
#> 8              Rubus hirtus    TRUE
#> 9                Abies alba    TRUE
#> 10        Oxalis acetosella    TRUE
#> # ... 999 more row(s)

summary() gives the match counts and lists the names that did not match:

summary(tax_apennine)
#> 1009 names checked: 1009 matched (100.0%), 0 not matched (0.0%).

4. Classify

resy_classify() evaluates the rules of every type for every plot and returns a resy_result object. scheme selects the bundled expert system.

res_apennine <- resy_classify(
  obs    = data_species,
  header = header,
  scheme = "Apennine-test"
)

Each plot is assigned to one type. resy_candidates() with wide = TRUE gives one row per plot; counting its classification column shows how many plots went to each type:

cand_wide <- resy_candidates(res_apennine, wide = TRUE)
table(cand_wide$classification)
#> 
#>  ?  F FB  N NG NS 
#> 92 33  8  6 20 41

A plot marked ? meets no type’s rule and is not classified. Here, 92 of the 200 plots remain unclassified. In these plots, all four indicator groups have at most 4% cover, below the lowest threshold in the rules (5%).

5. Inspect results

Candidate types for all plots

A plot often meets the rules of several types, for example a lower-level type and its parent. Each type has a priority in the expert system, and the plot is assigned to the type with the highest priority. resy_candidates() lists every type whose rule a plot meets, highest priority first. priority_rank numbers the priority levels of the expert system from the lowest upward. Use top_n to limit the number of types returned per plot.

cand_apennine <- resy_candidates(res_apennine, top_n = 3)
head(cand_apennine)
#>    plot_id   type priority priority_rank
#>     <char> <char>    <ord>         <int>
#> 1:    AM30      F        2             1
#> 2:    AN57      F        2             1
#> 3:    BE71     FB        5             3
#> 4:    BE71      F        2             1
#> 5:    BK34     NS        3             2
#> 6:    BK34      N        2             1

Plot-level details

resy_eval_plot() prints the full evidence for one plot: its species, which vegetation-type formulas evaluated to TRUE, and the type it is classified as. It then lists the lower-level types the plot did not reach, with the result of each of their conditions, which shows why the classification stopped at this level.

# Replace "AN57" with a PlotObservationID present in your data
resy_eval_plot(res_apennine, p = "AN57")
#> Types whose rule holds: F (priority 2)
#> Classified as F (Forest).
#> 
#> Plot AN57: 10 species
#>  species                 cover
#>  Fagus sylvatica         62.5 
#>  Vaccinium myrtillus     37.5 
#>  Abies alba               0.5 
#>  Oxalis acetosella        0.5 
#>  Sorbus aucuparia         0.5 
#>  Athyrium filix-femina    0.1 
#>  Dryopteris expansa       0.1 
#>  Gymnocarpium dryopteris  0.1 
#>  Polypodium vulgare       0.1 
#>  Prenanthes purpurea      0.1 
#> 
#> Why not a lower level of F:
#> 
#> FB    Beech-fir montane forest: rule not met
#>       Rule: [1] and [2]
#>       [1] met      total cover of Beech-forest-trees is 62.7%, needs more than 15%
#>                    Fagus sylvatica 62.5, Abies alba 0.5
#>       [2] not met  total cover of Beech-forest-herbs is 0.6%, needs more than 10%
#>                    Oxalis acetosella 0.5, Prenanthes purpurea 0.1

Passing type explains any other type in the same way, whether or not its rule holds for the plot:

resy_eval_plot(res_apennine, p = "AN57", type = "FB")
#> Types whose rule holds: F (priority 2)
#> Classified as F (Forest).
#> 
#> Plot AN57: 10 species
#>  species                 cover
#>  Fagus sylvatica         62.5 
#>  Vaccinium myrtillus     37.5 
#>  Abies alba               0.5 
#>  Oxalis acetosella        0.5 
#>  Sorbus aucuparia         0.5 
#>  Athyrium filix-femina    0.1 
#>  Dryopteris expansa       0.1 
#>  Gymnocarpium dryopteris  0.1 
#>  Polypodium vulgare       0.1 
#>  Prenanthes purpurea      0.1 
#> 
#> Why not a lower level of F:
#> 
#> FB    Beech-fir montane forest: rule not met
#>       Rule: [1] and [2]
#>       [1] met      total cover of Beech-forest-trees is 62.7%, needs more than 15%
#>                    Fagus sylvatica 62.5, Abies alba 0.5
#>       [2] not met  total cover of Beech-forest-herbs is 0.6%, needs more than 10%
#>                    Oxalis acetosella 0.5, Prenanthes purpurea 0.1
#> 
#> FB    Beech-fir montane forest: rule not met
#>       Rule: [1] and [2]
#>       [1] met      total cover of Beech-forest-trees is 62.7%, needs more than 15%
#>                    Fagus sylvatica 62.5, Abies alba 0.5
#>       [2] not met  total cover of Beech-forest-herbs is 0.6%, needs more than 10%
#>                    Oxalis acetosella 0.5, Prenanthes purpurea 0.1

Next steps

The classification above used an expert system without site data and species names that already match it. With your own plots, one of these usually comes next:

  • Your plots have coordinates and you want EUNIS habitat types: vignette("EUNIS") adds the ecoregion, country and coastal position from the coordinates and classifies the plots.
  • Your species names follow another taxonomy, such as GBIF or World Flora Online, and resy_check_taxonomy() reports many unmatched names: vignette("taxonomy") matches them to the names of the expert system.
  • Your plots have no altitude: vignette("altitude-vignette") takes the altitude that some EUNIS rules use from a separately downloaded elevation map.
  • You have your own expert system: resy_validate_esy() checks the file, and resy_add_classification() makes it available to resy_classify().
